A diferencia de todos los demás conciertos de Mozart, este no prevé una cadenza para el solista en su primer movimiento, sí en el Adagio.

editionReviews.archivedCredits:
This transcription of a relatively obscure operatic selection was motivated by the performance of a vocalist for whom I hold a great deal of respect and awe.

When I was a sophomore in high school, I was in City High School's production of Mary Poppins, which received a plethora of awards and recognition from the Iowa High School Musical Theatre Awards. I played the role of Mrs. Brill, which provided me with the first of two special recognition awards from the IHSMTA that I would obtain during my high school career (the second being from my senior year, in which I played the male role of Big Jule in Guys and Dolls).

In our production of Mary Poppins, the roles of Mary and Bert were double cast, with the evening pair each receiving well-deserved leading performer awards. However, I was keenly aware of the assured vocal maturity and musicianship of the matinée Mary, who was portrayed by Evelyn "Eddy" Galstad. While I had never worked with Eddy before, I was continuously stunned by her nuanced soprano voice. Eventually, she went off to Luther College to pursue a degree in vocal performance. Her vocal gifts were ultimately met with a well-deserved financial gift — the coveted Brudos Opera Prize.

Recipients of the Brudos Opera Prize get the opportunity to perform a solo recital in recognition of their achievements. Although Eddy was originally slated to perform her recital in May around the time of her graduation, it had to be rescheduled to October due to the ongoing pandemic. Luckily, I was able to witness her performance via Luther's livestreaming service. (Here's the link to the full recital: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2OjCjN2Pyl0)

As this was the opening number to the program (and was one of several works that I had never heard of previously), I decided to transcribe it in its full form to better appreciate the stylistic details and to further appreciate Eddy’s thrilling execution of Arne's swift, high-lying vocal line.

Das Lied der Deutschen, auch Deutschlandlied genannt, wurde von August Heinrich Hoffmann von Fallersleben am 26. August 1841 gedichtet. Nach der Wiedervereinigung wurde im Jahr 1991 die dritte Strophe zur Nationalhymne Deutschlands erklärt.

editionReviews.archivedCredits:
Will H. Vodery (or Will A. Vodery. I've seen both, but probably H) is an interesting composer. On the surface it's a name I doubt anyone will know, and I myself did not know either at first. I had done no prior research on him before preparing to upload this score, and I expected to find nothing of interest, if anything at all.

How wonderfully wrong I was.

All of the following info is taken from wikipedia, so take that as you will, but it goes as follows: Vodery was an african-american composer, with speedy beginnings. Born on October 8th, 1885, to a pianist (his mother), and a teacher at Lincoln University in Philadelphia (father). From an early age his family rented rooms to theater performers, exposing him to many talented performers at the turn of the century.

From there it is mostly uneventful. In 1910 he started serving as the musical director for performances at the Howard Theater in Washing D.C, up until a year later. Over a decade later he apparently started composing for several theater shows, I.E: From Dixie to Broadway, Show Boat, etc, nothing terribly interesting (at least to me).

But the two most significant parts are these: In 1922 he apparently worked with the infamous George Gershwin for a time, providing orchestrations for Gershwin's 'Blue Monday' opera.

Secondly, Vodery was also an important influence on - not joking - Duke Ellington. This description is getting rather long so I won't go until a whole lot more detail, but I will leave this: " Also in 1929, Vodery, in his capacity as Ziegfeld's musical supervisor, recommended Ellington for Show Girl." (Also a Gershwin musical).

I encourage you to read the whole thing here, and see if more can be found: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_Vodery It's rare that so much can be found on such an obscure composer, but it's a very pleasant surprise to learn he did more behind the scenes than one would expect.

editionReviews.archivedTitle: Double Violin Concerto in D Minor, RV 514
editionReviews.archivedCredits:
Please use the YouTube audio provided if possible. This piece requires human musicality—computer playing fails to do it justice.


(Unfortunately, due to a glitch that shifted my markings for when to switch to the next bar, you will need to manually scroll through the score. Sorry for any inconvenience caused by this.)


Go here to find the full score or any part as PDF files: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1FR-yHCniukTZJeHD7EhfqQBcEOdiFK7y?usp=sharing


Out of Vivaldi's twenty-eight (according to Wikipedia, which is not entirely reputable) known double violin concerti, this one stands out for several reasons, one of which being that all movements encompass concise themes and imitation; in fact, each movement introduces a theme in the first violins, followed by exact imitation in the second violins.

Note the first movement for its development. Vivaldi would typically leave the majority of development to the ritornello and introduce great amounts of new material in the soloists' parts; however, Vivaldi gradually morphs the soloists' melodies into new, exciting shapes throughout the movement.


Another interesting aspect of the concerto is its second movement's opening. The style is in stark contrast to nearly every slow movement Vivaldi wrote, the only similar slow movement I can think of being the andante from another double violin concerto, RV 313, which is fugal.


The third movement is intense and fiery, the fastest of the three movements, which is the usual tempo scheme for a Vivaldian concerto. Out of the three movements, it is the most "normal", but this does not make it any less valuable than the preceding movements.


I decided to copy down this piece for these reasons, as well as the fact that individual parts seem not to be available on the Internet. Enjoy!

This movement starts out with lilting and cheery melody that reminds one of the beautiful mountain setting where Brahms wrote his 3rd symphony.   Upon hearing this music, one can almost see the shepherds tending their flocks in an alpine meadow. Suddenly the mood  changes as the music transitions without warning into a vigorous dancelike presto section requiring quick and delicate string playing.

The initial allegretto melody comes back again in the middle of the movement in the form of a march-like minor key variation that interrupts the festivities like a funeral procession invading a lively party.  But the sombre mood does not last long. After another lively section in 3/8 time, the movement ends with a calm restatement of the initial melody.

Here's what Wikipedia has to say about Brahm's first symphony:

"Brahms began composing his first symphony in 1854, but much of his work underwent radical changes.  The long gestation of the symphony may be attributed to two factors. First, Brahms' self-critical fastidiousness led him to destroy many of his early works. Second, there was an expectation from Brahms' friends and the public that he would continue "Beethoven's inheritance" and produce a symphony of commensurate dignity and intellectual scope—an expectation that Brahms felt he could not fulfill easily in view of the monumental reputation of Beethoven."

"The value and importance of Brahms' achievements were recognized by Vienna's most powerful critic, the staunchly conservative Eduard Hanslick.  The conductor Hans von Bülow was moved in 1877 to call the symphony "Beethoven's Tenth", due to perceived similarities between the work and various compositions of Beethoven.  It is often remarked that there is a strong resemblance between the main theme of the finale of Brahms' First Symphony and the main theme of the finale of Beethoven's Ninth Symphony. Also, Brahms uses the rhythm of the "fate" motto from the opening of Beethoven's Fifth Symphony. This rather annoyed Brahms; he felt that this amounted to accusations of plagiarism, whereas he saw his use of Beethoven's idiom in this symphony as an act of conscious homage. Brahms himself said, when comment was made on the similarity with Beethoven, "any ass can see that."  Nevertheless, this work is still often referred to as "Beethoven's Tenth".  However, Brahms' horn theme, with the "fate" rhythm, was noted in a letter to Clara Schumann (dated 1868), overheard in an alphorn's playing. "


In this symphony he uses a relatively simple orchestration with A  limited variety of brass and percussion.  There are no tubas or trombones  and only timpani for percussion.  A trio of trombones does make a dramatic appearance in the last movement of this symphony. The brass instruments are used lightly for subtle effects, not too much fortissimo blasting away for the most part.

The winds are lushly scored with doubled parts in a dense, close harmony. Some composers say that his wind orchestration is a bit too thick, but that is a matter of opinion.  The addition of the contrabassoon adds weight to the woodwind section.

The strings are also lushly scored with many double stops and independent melodic lines. The basses often go their own way from the cellos.
